paper.title: Close Separable C∗-Algebras, Without Spatial Conjugacy
paper.html:
Abstract

We disprove the separable C∗-algebraic spatial form of the Kadison–Kastler conjecture. For every ε>0, we construct unital, norm-separable C∗-algebras on a common separable complex Hilbert space, with the same identity and Kadison–Kastler distance less than ε, that are not conjugate by any unitary. The two algebras have the same von Neumann closure.

1 Introduction

For C∗-algebras A,B⊆B(H), write A1​ and B1​ for their closed unit balls. Their Kadison–Kastler distance is
dKK​(A,B)=max{a∈A1​sup​b∈B1​inf​∥a−b∥,b∈B1​sup​a∈A1​inf​∥b−a∥}.(1)
The spatial form of the perturbation problem asks whether sufficiently close algebras must be related by uAu∗=B for a unitary u∈B(H). Kadison and Kastler initiated this problem in [6]. In its separable C∗-algebraic form, one asks for a constant δ>0 valid for all norm-separable C∗-algebras on separable Hilbert spaces; no bound on ∥u−I∥ is required. The following theorem resolves negatively this separable C∗-algebraic spatial form of the Kadison–Kastler conjecture, even for unital algebras with a common identity.
Theorem 1.1.
For every ε>0 there are a separable complex Hilbert space H and unital, norm-separable C∗-algebras A,B⊆B(H) with common identity IH​ such that
dKK​(A,B)<ε,A′′=B′′,
but no unitary u∈B(H) satisfies uAu∗=B.
The scope of this statement is important. Johnson constructed arbitrarily close separable nuclear algebras for which implementing unitaries cannot be chosen close to the identity [5]; those examples are nevertheless spatially conjugate. Choi and Christensen constructed arbitrarily close nonisomorphic algebras [2], but norm nonseparability is essential to those examples. These distinctions, and the resulting separable spatial formulation, are discussed in [3]. In the positive direction, Christensen, Sinclair, Smith, White, and Winter proved spatial conjugacy for sufficiently close separable nuclear C∗-algebras on a separable Hilbert space [3, Theorem~4]; see [4, Theorem~5.4] for the full proof. Theorem 1.1 imposes no nuclearity assumption. It makes no assertion of abstract nonisomorphism and does not give a counterexample for von Neumann algebras.
The construction. We first isolate a way to turn an obstruction for inclusions into an obstruction to arbitrary spatial conjugacy. Let D⊆B(L) be unital, norm-separable, and have scalar center. For unital subalgebras P,Q⊆D, consider the algebra
ED​(P)={(xn​):xn​∈D, xn​⟶p∈P in norm}
acting diagonally on ⨁n≥1​L. Changing P changes only the condition at the limit. The coordinate projections are intrinsic minimal central projections of this algebra. Consequently, a unitary conjugating ED​(P) onto ED​(Q) must permute the coordinates and normalize D on every coordinate. Pulling back constant sequences then forces each finite family in Q to be a simultaneous norm limit of families in unitary conjugates of P by normalizers of D.
Write D′ for the commutant of D on L, consisting of the bounded operators commuting with every element of D. The obstruction we use is the equality
​i∑​pi​zi​​B(L)​=​i∑​pi​⊗zi​​B(L⊗L)​,pi​∈P,zi​∈D′.(2)
This equality is invariant under normalizers of D and passes to simultaneous finite-family norm limits. We construct very close subalgebras P0​,Pt​⊆D for which it holds for P0​ but fails for Pt​. In fact, P0​ and Pt​ themselves are conjugate by a unitary close to the identity. The obstruction concerns their positions inside D, and the sequence construction makes it an obstruction to every spatial conjugacy of the resulting algebras.
For the close inclusions we use a real-parameter deformation of the regular representation of the free group on countably many generators. This representation-theoretic ingredient belongs to the Pytlik–Szwarc family [7]; its uniform-topology behavior at the regular representation is discussed by Burger, Ozawa, and Thom [1, Theorem~4.6]. We give a direct tree construction and prove the uniform estimate needed here. The additional mechanism is the combination of the relative tensor-norm test with the convergent-sequence reduction. The reduction is stated separately, so it can be used for other pairs of inclusions.
Section 2 proves the reduction. Section 3 constructs the representations, and Section 4 establishes the tensor-norm obstruction. Section 5 assembles the counterexamples. All Hilbert spaces are complex, and all operator tensor products below act on the indicated Hilbert-space tensor products. No abstract choice of C∗-tensor norm is needed. Unital subalgebras are understood to contain the identity of their ambient operator algebra.

2 A convergent-sequence obstruction

We explain how the limit condition records an inclusion P⊆D. The resulting algebras preserve the distance between limit algebras, but their spatial conjugacies are constrained by the coordinate algebra D.
Proposition 2.1.
Let L be a nonzero separable Hilbert space, let D⊆B(L) be a unital norm-separable C∗-algebra with Z(D)=CIL​, and let P,Q⊆D be unital C∗-subalgebras containing IL​. On H=⨁n≥1​L, define
ED​(P)={(xn​)n≥1​:xn​∈D, xn​→p∈P in norm},(3)
and define ED​(Q) similarly. Then:
  1. These are unital norm-separable C∗-algebras with common identity, and
    dKK​(ED​(P),ED​(Q))=dKK​(P,Q).(4)
  2. If a unitary conjugates ED​(P) onto ED​(Q), there are unitaries Un​∈B(L) with Un​DUn∗​=D such that, for every b∈Q, some pb​∈P satisfies
    ∥b−Un​pb​Un∗​∥⟶0.(5)
    The same sequence (Un​) works for every b.
  3. The two algebras have the same commutant, and hence the same von Neumann closure.
Proof.
A norm-convergent sequence is bounded, so (3) defines a diagonal operator on H, with norm supn​∥xn​∥. Algebra operations and adjoints preserve the limit condition, and the constant identity belongs to the algebra. To check norm closedness, suppose x(k)→x in the supremum norm, with coordinate limits pk​∈P. Then
∥pk​−pj​∥≤nsup​​xn(k)​−xn(j)​​.
Thus pk​→p∈P. The estimate
∥xn​−p∥≤​xn​−xn(k)​​+​xn(k)​−pk​​+∥pk​−p∥
shows that xn​→p. Moreover,
ED​(P)=c0​(N,D)+{(p,p,…):p∈P}.(6)
The two summands are norm-separable: P is a subspace of the separable metric space D, and finite-support sequences from a countable dense subset of D are dense in c0​(N,D). Their sum is norm-separable.
For the metric assertion, write α(P,Q)=supp∈P1​​dist(p,Q1​). Given a contraction x∈ED​(P) with limit p and η>0, choose q∈Q1​ with ∥p−q∥<α(P,Q)+η, and choose N so that supn>N​∥xn​−p∥<η. Keeping the first N entries of x and putting q thereafter gives a contraction y∈ED​(Q) with ∥x−y∥<α(P,Q)+2η. This proves the upper bound for the directed distance. Conversely, for a constant contraction (p,p,…) and any contraction y∈ED​(Q) with limit q∈Q1​,
∥(p,p,…)−y∥=nsup​∥p−yn​∥≥∥p−q∥≥dist(p,Q1​).
Taking infima and suprema proves equality of the directed distances. Interchanging P,Q gives (4).
Let en​ be the projection onto the nth copy of L. Every en​ is a central element of ED​(P). Conversely, a central element (xn​) commutes with all finite-support D-valued sequences, so each xn​ lies in Z(D)=CIL​. Thus the center consists exactly of convergent scalar sequences. Every nonzero central projection contains an en​, and hence the minimal nonzero central projections are precisely the en​. The same holds for ED​(Q).
If SED​(P)S∗=ED​(Q), conjugation by S therefore permutes the projections en​. Its restriction from the nth coordinate to its image is a unitary Un​:L→L. The corresponding coordinate corners of both algebras are exactly D, since every finitely supported D-valued sequence is allowed. Consequently Un​DUn∗​=D. For b∈Q, pull back the constant sequence (b,b,…) under S. Its nth entry is Un∗​bUn​, regardless of the coordinate permutation. It belongs to ED​(P), so its entries converge in norm to some pb​∈P. This is equivalent to (5) and proves (ii).
Finally, an operator commuting with ED​(P) commutes with all en​, so it is block diagonal. Commutation with the finite-support D corners means that each block lies in D′. These conditions are also sufficient, and do not depend on P. Thus both commutants equal
{(zn​):zn​∈D′, nsup​∥zn​∥<∞}.
This proves (iii).
∎
We next give a concrete condition preserved by the approximation in Proposition 2.1(ii).
Definition 2.2.
For a unital inclusion P⊆D⊆B(L), say that P has the spatial tensor-norm identity relative to D if
​i=1∑m​pi​zi​​B(L)​=​i=1∑m​pi​⊗zi​​B(L⊗L)​(7)
for every positive integer m, all p1​,…,pm​∈P, and all z1​,…,zm​∈D′.
Lemma 2.3.
Let P,Q⊆D⊆B(L) be unital C∗-algebras. The identity in Definition 2.2 is preserved by conjugating P with any unitary normalizing D. If (Un​) is a sequence of unitaries in B(L) satisfying Un​DUn∗​=D and every b∈Q admits the approximation (5), then the identity for P implies the identity for Q.
Proof.
If UDU∗=D, then UD′U∗=D′. For qi​=Upi​U∗ and zi​∈D′, apply (7) to pi​ and U∗zi​U. Conjugate its product sum by U and its tensor sum by U⊗U. This gives (7) for qi​,zi​.
Now fix finite families bi​∈Q and zi​∈D′. Put qi,n​=Un​pbi​​Un∗​. For each n, the first part gives the identity for the entire list (qi,n​)i​, since its entries all lie in Un​PUn∗​. Both errors
​i∑​(qi,n​−bi​)zi​​,​i∑​(qi,n​−bi​)⊗zi​​
are at most ∑i​∥qi,n​−bi​∥∥zi​∥, which tends to zero. Taking the limit proves the identity for the prescribed families in Q and D′.
∎
Corollary 2.4.
Under the hypotheses of Proposition 2.1, suppose that P has the spatial tensor-norm identity relative to D, whereas Q does not. Then ED​(P) and ED​(Q) are not spatially conjugate. If W∈B(L) is unitary and WPW∗=Q, then nevertheless
dKK​(ED​(P),ED​(Q))≤2∥W−IL​∥.
Proof.
A spatial conjugacy would give the unitaries in Proposition 2.1(ii), contradicting Lemma 2.3. For the distance bound, p↦WpW∗ bijects the closed unit balls and
∥WpW∗−p∥≤2∥p∥∥W−IL​∥.
Apply Proposition 2.1(i).
∎
The unitary W used for the distance estimate is not required to normalize D. Indeed, under the stated tensor-norm obstruction, no unitary normalizing D can conjugate P onto Q.

3 A uniformly small free-group deformation

We now construct the representations used to produce the inclusions in Corollary 2.4. Let G be the free group on the countable set {s1​,s2​,…}, let e denote its identity, and put K=ℓ2(G). On its usual orthonormal basis define
λ(g)δx​=δgx​,ρ(g)δx​=δxg−1​.(8)
Both are unitary representations, and every left translation commutes with every right translation. The group G is countable, so K is separable.
The following elementary version of the real Pytlik–Szwarc deformation [7; 1] records exactly the coefficient and uniform estimate that the proof needs.
Lemma 3.1.
For every 0<t<1, there is a unitary representation πt​:G→B(K) such that, with r=1−t2​,
⟨πt​(si​)δe​,δe​⟩g∈Gsup​∥πt​(g)−λ(g)∥​=t(i≥1),≤c(t),c(t)=2(1−r)+1−tt​+t.​(9)(10)​
In particular, c(t)→0 as t↓0.
Proof.
Use the tree of reduced words with edges given by right multiplication by a generator or its inverse, rooted at e. Its distance is d(x,y)=∣x−1y∣, so left translations preserve distance. For x=e, let p(x) be the neighbor of x toward e, obtained by deleting the last letter of its reduced word. Recursively define
ξe​=δe​,ξx​=tξp(x)​+rδx​(x=e).(11)
These are unit vectors supported on their root paths. If z is the last common vertex of the root paths to x and y, the common-support components are td(x,z)ξz​ and td(y,z)ξz​, respectively. The remaining supports are disjoint. Hence
⟨ξx​,ξy​⟩=td(x,y).(12)
Also δe​=ξe​ and δx​=(ξx​−tξp(x)​)/r for x=e, so their span is dense. The assignment ξx​↦ξgx​ preserves every finite Gram matrix by (12). It therefore defines an isometry on the span, and the inverse assignment for g−1 makes the extension unitary. Denote this unitary by πt​(g). The representation law holds on the dense span and hence on K. Since πt​(si​)δe​=ξsi​​=tδe​+rδsi​​, (9) follows.
It remains to prove that the perturbation is uniformly small over all group elements, rather than just over the generators. Fix g=e, write h0​=e,h1​,…,hl​=g for its root path, and put T=πt​(g)λ(g)∗. For y=g, (11) gives
Tδy​=rξy​−tξgp(g−1y)​​.(13)
The vertex gp(g−1y) is the neighbor of y toward g. If y is off the path [e,g], this neighbor is also p(y), the neighbor toward e; see Figure 1. Thus Tδy​=δy​ off that path. On the path, the neighbor toward g of hk​, for k<l, is hk+1​, so
Tδhk​​=rξhk​​−tδhk+1​​(0≤k<l),Tδhl​​=ξhl​​.(14)
Let Mg​=span{δhk​​:0≤k≤l}. On this space define the truncated shift Sδhk​​=δhk+1​​ for k<l and Sδhl​​=0, and put Xδhk​​=ξhk​​. For R=diag(1,r,…,r), the recursion gives
X=R(I−tS∗)−1.(15)
Indeed, its kth column is tkδe​+r∑j=1k​tk−jδhj​​. Since ∥S∥≤1 and ∥R∥=1,
∥X−I∥≤∥R−I∥+∥R∥j=1∑∞​tj≤1−r+1−tt​.(16)
Writing R′=diag(r,…,r,1), (14) becomes T∣Mg​​=XR′−tS. Therefore
​T∣Mg​​−I​​≤∥(X−I)R′∥+∥R′−I∥+t∥S∥≤2(1−r)+1−tt​+t=c(t).​
The same bound holds on K, since T is the identity on Mg⊥​. Multiplication by λ(g) proves (10). For g=e the difference is zero, so the supremum includes this case as well.
∎
Remark 3.2.
Only the operator X on a single finite path is used in the estimate. On this infinitely branching tree, the global map δx​↦ξx​ need not be bounded: the vectors ξsi​​ all have root coefficient t. The Gram-matrix construction of πt​ does not require such a global bounded map.

4 Close inclusions distinguished by a tensor norm

Fix 0<t<1, let πt​ be given by Lemma 3.1, and write π0​=λ. We construct a common coordinate algebra D and subalgebras P0​,Pt​ satisfying Corollary 2.4. First we record the absorption calculation that will be used both for closeness and for the tensor-norm estimate.
Lemma 4.1 (Absorption).
Let σ be a unitary representation of G on a nonzero Hilbert space J. The operator
Wσ​(δx​⊗v)=δx​⊗σ(x)v(x∈G, v∈J)
is unitary on K⊗J and satisfies
Wσ​(λ(g)⊗IJ​)Wσ∗​=λ(g)⊗σ(g)(g∈G).(17)
Proof.
The operator is the orthogonal direct sum of the unitaries σ(x). On δx​⊗v, the left side of (17) equals
δgx​⊗σ(gx)σ(x)∗v=δgx​⊗σ(g)v.□
∎
On L=K⊗K, put
Qa​(g)=λ(g)⊗πa​(g),Pa​=C∗(Qa​(g):g∈G)(a=0,t).(18)
For the matrix units Exy​δz​=1{z=y}​δx​ on K, define D⊆B(L) to be generated by
λ(g)⊗IK​,IK​⊗π0​(g),IK​⊗πt​(g)(g∈G),IK​⊗Exy​(x,y∈G).(19)
The generators include the identity, and P0​,Pt​⊆D. All three algebras are norm-separable, since their generating sets are countable.
Lemma 4.2.
The algebra D in (19) has scalar center, and
D′={Y⊗IK​:Y∈λ(G)′}.(20)
There is a unitary W∈B(L) such that
WP0​W∗=Pt​,∥W−IL​∥≤c(t).(21)
Proof.
Commutation with all IK​⊗Exy​ forces a bounded operator to be Y⊗IK​: commutation with the diagonal matrix units removes off-diagonal blocks, and commutation with the remaining units makes the diagonal blocks identical. The first-factor generators then impose exactly Y∈λ(G)′. Such operators commute with all the second-factor generators, proving (20). In particular, ρ(g)⊗IK​∈D′.
If Y⊗IK​∈Z(D), then Y commutes with λ(G) by (20). It also commutes with ρ(G), since Y⊗IK​ belongs to D and the right translations belong to D′. Thus Yδe​ is invariant under λ(g)ρ(g), which acts on the basis by conjugation x↦gxg−1. Every nonidentity conjugacy class in G is infinite: conjugate a fixed nonidentity reduced word by distinct generators absent from that word. A square-summable vector invariant under conjugation must therefore be supported at e. Write Yδe​=αδe​. Commuting with left translations gives Yδx​=αδx​ for every x, proving Z(D)=CIL​.
For the final assertion, Lemma 4.1 shows that W=Wπt​​Wπ0​∗​ sends every Q0​(g) to Qt​(g) by conjugation. Moreover, the direct-sum description of these unitaries gives
∥W−IL​∥=∥Wπt​​−Wπ0​​∥=x∈Gsup​∥πt​(x)−λ(x)∥≤c(t).□
∎
Lemma 4.3.
The inclusion P0​⊆D has the spatial tensor-norm identity.
Proof.
Define a unitary on L by
V(v⊗δx​)=λ(x)∗v⊗δx​.
It commutes with every element of D′ by (20). On elementary vectors one computes
VQ0​(g)V∗(v⊗δx​)=v⊗δgx​.
Thus VP0​V∗=IK​⊗C∗(λ(G)). Given finite families pi​∈P0​ and zi​∈D′, write
Vpi​V∗=IK​⊗Xi​,zi​=Yi​⊗IK​.
Conjugation by V gives
​i∑​pi​zi​​=​i∑​Yi​⊗Xi​​.
On L⊗L=K⊗4, conjugation by V⊗IL​ gives
​i∑​pi​⊗zi​​=​i∑​IK​⊗Xi​⊗Yi​⊗IK​​=​i∑​Yi​⊗Xi​​.
The last equality permutes the four tensor factors and uses the fact that tensoring with a nonzero identity operator does not change norm. This proves (7).
∎
For Pt​, the identity will fail because the product norm has a lower bound linear in the number of generators, while absorption gives a square-root upper bound on the tensor norm.
Lemma 4.4.
For every positive integer m,
​i=1∑m​λ(si​)​≤2m​.(22)
Proof.
Let Fi​ be the orthogonal projection onto the closed span of words beginning with si−1​. The Fi​ are pairwise orthogonal. Write λ(si​)=Ai​+Bi​, where
Ai​=λ(si​)(IK​−Fi​),Bi​=λ(si​)Fi​.
There is no cancellation when si​ is prepended to a word not beginning with si−1​. Thus the range of Ai​ consists of vectors supported on words beginning with si​, and these ranges are mutually orthogonal. For every v∈K,
​i∑​Ai​v​2=i∑​∥(IK​−Fi​)v∥2≤m∥v∥2,
while
​i∑​Bi​v​≤i∑​∥Fi​v∥≤m​(i∑​∥Fi​v∥2)1/2≤m​∥v∥.
Adding the two bounds proves (22).
∎
Lemma 4.5.
For every 0<t<1, the inclusion Pt​⊆D fails the spatial tensor-norm identity.
Proof.
Choose an integer m>4/t2, so mt>2m​, and take
pi​=Qt​(si​),zi​=ρ(si​)⊗IK​,1≤i≤m.
These belong to Pt​ and D′, respectively. Since λ(si​)ρ(si​)δe​=δe​, (9) implies
​i∑​pi​zi​​≥​⟨(i∑​pi​zi​)(δe​⊗δe​),δe​⊗δe​⟩​=mt.(23)
On the other hand, the tensor sum on L⊗L is
i=1∑m​λ(si​)⊗πt​(si​)⊗ρ(si​)⊗IK​.
Apply Lemma 4.1 to the representation σ=πt​⊗ρ⊗1 on K⊗3, where 1 is the trivial representation on the last copy of K. Together with Lemma 4.4, it gives
​i∑​pi​⊗zi​​=​i=1∑m​λ(si​)​≤2m​<mt.(24)
Equations (23) and (24) contradict the identity for this finite list.
∎

5 The counterexamples

Proof of Theorem 1.1.
Given ε>0, choose 0<t<1 so small that 2c(t)<ε. Use the algebras P0​,Pt​⊆D⊆B(L) from Section 4, and put
H=n≥1⨁​L,A=ED​(P0​),B=ED​(Pt​).
The space H is separable. Lemma 4.2 supplies the scalar center of D, so Proposition 2.1 shows that A,B are unital norm-separable C∗-algebras with common identity and that A′′=B′′. The same lemma supplies a unitary W with WP0​W∗=Pt​ and ∥W−IL​∥≤c(t). By Corollary 2.4,
dKK​(A,B)≤2c(t)<ε.
Finally, Lemmas 4.3 and 4.5 show that the relative tensor-norm identity holds for P0​ but not for Pt​. Corollary 2.4 therefore excludes every unitary conjugating A onto B.
∎
The common ideal c0​(N,D) makes the von Neumann closures agree, while the norm-limit condition retains the distinction between the two inclusions.
